we do not adhere fully to the Lord Ordinary’s approach in requiring a further adjustment in
the husband’s favour as regards the La Mondiale bond.  The balancing payment  in order to
achieve equal sharing would be £15,586.29.  On a broad approach, we have assessed the
appropriate balancing payment to be one of £10,000.

15

[46]
The wife’s share in 13b has increased in value by £7,500 since the relevant date.  It is
the current value of an asset that is used for the purposes of a transfer of property order –
1985 Act, section 10(3A). Taking that into account we have concluded that we should order
the husband to pay a capital sum of £17,500 to the wife.
[47]
The Lord Ordinary did not deal explicitly with certain of the conclusions directed to
question of whether the conservatory was within the title of 13b.  He did, however, make a
finding of fact and law that the conservatory formed part of 13b, and fell within the title to
13b, perhaps better described as 13, under exception of 13a.  On the order that the
Lord Ordinary made for transfer of the wife’s one-half pro indiviso share of 13b to the
husband, the husband will have title to the whole of the property – 13a and 13b.  If there are
difficulties which still require to be resolved arising from the voluntary registration of the
title to 13a purporting to include the conservatory, those will be more straightforward to
remedy where there is no party other than the husband with an interest in the matter.
[48]
We will recall  the interlocutor of the Lord Ordinary.  In relation to  the transfer of the
wife’s share of 13b to the husband we shall specify that the transfer is to be in exchange for a
discharge of her liabilities under the standard security in favour of Virgin Money.
[49]
The interlocutor that we  pronounce will also dispose of the pursuer’s first and fourth
conclusions, which are for divorce and for transfer of the wife’s share in 13b, and of the
defender’s first conclusion, which is for payment of a capital sum.  We will dismiss all of the
other conclusions for the parties.

Expenses
[50]
Senior counsel for the wife submitted that in the event that her reclaiming motion
succeeded, this court should make a finding of no expenses due to or by as between the

16

husband and the wife, both in respect of the reclaiming motion and the proceedings before
the Lord Ordinary.
[51]
The wife has been successful in the reclaiming motion.  So far as the expenses in the
Outer House are concerned, the Lord Ordinary made the award of expenses that he did
partly because the husband had offered, on the morning of the proof, to settle on the basis
that the wife transfer her one half share of 13b to him, and that the parties otherwise retain
their respective assets and liabilities.  In the event, the Lord Ordinary’s order was more
favourable to the husband than the offer he had made.  The Lord Ordinary also considered
that there was divided success between the parties.
[52]
We have recalled that part of the Lord Ordinary’s interlocutor that required payment
of a capital sum by the wife to the husband.  It is not appropriate that she should be found
liable, even as an assisted person, to the husband in respect of half of the expenses of the
proof.  We will therefore recall the Lord Ordinary’s interlocutor insofar as it makes provision
for that liability, and will substitute a finding of no expenses to or by the husband or the
wife.

The Minuter
[53]
The husband was unsuccessful in his application to have the loan and standard
security set aside.  He has not reclaimed in relation to the Lord Ordinary’s conclusion about
that matter.  The husband submits that the by order hearing on 15 August 2025 was
necessitated by “procedurally incompetent and misleading submissions advanced by [the
wife] and entertained by the court”.  Those submissions appear to relate to a concern on the
part of the Lord Ordinary as to whether the amended pleadings had been served on

17

Virgin Money, and as to the position of Virgin Money in relation to the transfer of the wife’s
share of 13b to the husband.
[54]
The Lord Ordinary records at para [118] of his opinion that the husband sought a
continuation of the hearing on 15 August 2025.  As a result of that continuation, the minuter
required to appear on a further occasion.  The matter that concerned the Lord Ordinary was
not one in which the minuter was directly interested.  It cannot be said that the decision of
the Lord Ordinary was irrational or otherwise vitiated by the sort of error that would permit
us to interfere with his discretion in the matter.
[55]
Turning to the husband’s submission that the Lord Ordinary should not have
anonymised the minuter, it is clear that the Lord Ordinary wished to protect the privacy of
the parties’ children.  The minuter was someone known personally to the parties as a friend
and member of their social circle.  It is reasonable to anonymise her to mitigate the risk of
jigsaw identification of the children.

Postscript
[56]
Paragraphs 90 to 122 of the Lord Ordinary’s opinion deal with matters which arose at
by order hearings after the proof.  It is desirable that the published opinion after proof be
identical to that issued to parties before any post-proof by order hearings:  Foster v Foster
2024 SC 99, para [45].  Although the Lord Ordinary in the present case did not issue an
opinion in draft, similar considerations apply to the practice adopted here.  The
Lord Ordinary’s opinion is his final opinion on the matters before him at proof, and should
ordinarily be published at the same time as it is issued to the parties.  There should be no
room for any potential confusion between what has been decided at proof and what comes

18

to be decided afterwards.  If there is a need for an opinion setting out the Lord Ordinary’s
reasoning on issues that arise after proof, a separate opinion should be prepared.  We note
that the second appendix to the Lord Ordinary’s opinion appears to have been prepared in
the light of submissions made to him at a by order hearing:  see para [104].

title: Fiona Drouet and others against BTO Solicitors LLP
text:
OUTER HOUSE, COURT OF SESSION
[2026] CSOH 66
A93/24
OPINION OF LORD CUBIE
In the cause
FIONA DROUET AND OTHERS
Pursuers
against
BTO SOLICITORS LLP
Defenders
Pursuers:  Elis KC;  Jones Whyte
Defenders:  Shand KC;  Beale & Company Solicitors LLP

14 July 2026
Background
[1]
This is an action arising from admitted negligence by the defenders who failed to
lodge a summons for calling as a result of which, an action by the current pursuers became
time barred against the then defender Angus Milligan.  The defenders in this case accept
that the failure was negligent, but assert that there was no loss sustained by any pursuer.
[2]
The pursuers in this action raised proceedings seeking to persuade the court that it
should exercise its discretion, to allow the action to nevertheless proceed.  The
Lord Ordinary (Drouet v Milligan [2024] CSOH 32) did not allow the action to proceed other

2
than by the first pursuer Fiona Drouet in her capacity as the parent and guardian of the
siblings of the deceased;  quoad ultra, he granted decree of absolvitor.
[3]
The Lord Ordinary described the arguments as finely balanced; one of the factors
taken into account was the possibility of an action for professional negligence against the
defenders about which the Lord Ordinary said “…it is difficult to imagine a more
straightforward case of professional negligence…” (para [66]).
[4]
The Lord Ordinary held that there were insufficiently cogent grounds in order to
allow the claims to proceed:  decree of absolvitor was granted, and he found the pursuers to
be jointly and severally liable for the expenses of the defender Angus Milligan; these
expenses have now been taxed by the auditor.  The pursuers also incurred fees to those
instructed to deal with the earlier action.  Mr Milligan has sought to enforce payment of
expenses.
[5]
The enforcement of the award of expenses, triggered some incidental procedure in
this case.  The pursuers inter alia seek to recover that sum from the defenders by way of
summary decree.  The pursuers wish to recover from these defenders the actual sum due to
be paid by them jointly and severally as a result of the unsuccessful action.
[6]
In simple terms, the pursuers offer to prove that there is one contract between the
pursuers and the defenders in relation to the provision of legal services.  The initial
conclusions in the summons were, as would be expected, one conclusion in relation to each
pursuer.
[7]
However, the pursuer considered that the individual conclusions were not apt in
relation to recovering the expenses which they say are due to the defender in the original
action and in relation to the sums due to be paid by them in respect of their own legal
advisers.  They accordingly seek to amend.  This minute of amendment was prompted by

3
the defenders’ note of argument in anticipation of a debate.  The note argued, that the
pursuers who, pending amendment, each only make claims for the damage suffered by
them separately, fail to specify the amount of expenses incurred by them individually in
respect of the preliminary proof on time bar.  The defenders argued that each pursuer
cannot individually sue for the whole of the liability in expenses, and the pursuers have
failed to specify which proportion of such sums is each particular pursuer's share.
In response the pursuers now seek to add joint conclusions for the two sums said to be due
by the pursuers as a group.
[8]
The defenders oppose the allowance of the amendment, on the ground of
incompetence and/or prescription.  In the first instance they attack the mechanism by which
the pursuers seek to recover the sums, arguing that the attempt to recover by the new
conclusions sought to be introduced by the pursuers is incompetent.
[9]
The minute of amendment of the pursuers seeks to add two new conclusions for
payment by the defenders to the pursuers jointly.  The new first conclusion is for the sum of
the expenses for which the pursuers are jointly and severally liable to Angus Milligan
arising from the preliminary proof for which they were found jointly and severally liable to
Mr Milligan.  The new second conclusion is made up of the expenses which the pursuers
themselves incurred for running the preliminary proof and the fees expended in respect of
the first summons which were rendered abortive by the defenders' failure.
[10]
The balance of the minute of amendment proposes changes to the articles of
condescendence, mainly to support the new conclusions and to also introduce averments in
relation to the new first conclusion which would permit an application by the pursuers for
an interim order in terms of section 47(2) of the Court of Session Act 1988.

4
Submissions for the pursuers
[11]
It is submitted that the minute of amendment for the pursuers more clearly focuses
the dispute between the parties.  No issue is raised which ought to lead to the court
exercising its discretion so as to refuse to receive the minute of amendment.  The proposed
amendment for the pursuers introduces no facts about which the defenders are not aware.
The defenders have for a long time held both a copy of the closed record in the Drouet v
Milligan action, and a copy of the detailed account of expenses incurred by Jones Whyte on
behalf of the pursuers in respect of the preliminary proof.  The minute of amendment is, the
pursuers say, in essence a reformulation of part of the pursuers' case in relation to damages.
[12]
In the pursuers’ submission, it is common for more than one pursuer to seek a
remedy in a single conclusion.  It commonly occurs in claims for damages to property, or
remedies in respect of a property where there are joint owners, whether that remedy is for
implement or for damages, for breach of contract where the pursuers have suffered a single
loss for failure in performance of a contract in which both (or more) of the pursuers are
parties.
[13]
In the case of co-owners of property or rights, it is normally regarded as compulsory
for all co-owners to conjoin in an action:  Stair Encyclopaedia Volume 18 paragraph 29.
In the case of damages by contracting parties there are circumstances where the contracting
parties, all have an indivisible interest in the remedy and a single conclusion is competent.
The competency of such a joint conclusion is clear.  Whether in a particular case any
pursuers can justify a joint remedy resolves into a question of relevancy.  Reference was
made to the decision of the Lord Ordinary in Tayside Contracts v Geddes 2014 SLT 764; this
case related to a joint committee, formed by the combining together of three local
authorities, who sought damages from aggregate suppliers in respect of an alleged breach of

5
contract.  The defenders sought dismissal of the action as incompetent, on the basis that the
joint committee did not have an independent legal personality, and although the local
authorities had been named in the instance, they were not designed separately, but rather as
a collective entity.  The Lord Ordinary determined that the action was not incompetent,
saying:
“…[28] The result is that Tayside Contracts, though not having its own legal
personality, can enter into contracts with third parties and carry out other acts in
discharge of its functions, all as authorised by ss.56 and 57 of the 1973 Act.  In these
circumstances it makes sense that any litigation of the present kind should be framed
in the name of the constituent councils acting together under the designation of
Tayside Contracts.  I see no difficulty with the three councils, on that basis, seeking
payment of a single sum by way of damages, which will be payable to the joint
committee and thereafter accounted for in the agreed manner.  No individual council
has any right to an identifiable share or part of the damages, but rather the whole
sum is payable to the joint committee as the contracting party.  I consider that all of
this is implicit in and authorised by the relevant statutory provisions.  It may be that
Tayside Contracts can be thought of as ‘a legal entity’ similar to that described by
Lord Keith of Avonholm in the context of a trade union in Bonsor v Musicians Union
at [1956] A.C., pp.150ff.  That said, if the suit was at the hand of the contracting third
party, I doubt if the claim would be constrained to exclude diligence against the
property of the member councils.  Having decided that the action as framed is
competent and appropriate, I shall repel the defenders' first plea in law and put the
case out for a hearing in terms of Rule of Court 47.12 in order to determine further
procedure….”

[14]
From that, the pursuers submitted that the indivisible nature of the sum sought
justified the separate conclusion for this sum;  the legislative background was not
fundamental to the procedural point being made;  that a single conclusion in relation to
more than one pursuer was competent, depending on the circumstances.  The defender
should not be entitled to deprive the pursuers of the right to recover if they have to pay.
The defender cannot hold the pursuers to some obligation to provide an artificial pro-rata
calculation.

6
[15]
The pursuers submitted, that the cases referred to by the defenders in their own note,
were concerned with different questions, not the question of when and whether a conclusion
with more than one pursuer suing jointly is competent.
[16]
The case of McNeil v NCB 1966 SC 72 is concerned with the question of whether a
tender lodged by defenders of a single sum in respect of a mother and daughter suing in one
action but with separate conclusions, was an effective tender.  In that case it was confirmed,
that a tender for a single sum to cover the individual claims of relatives was not an effective
tender.  The claims were separate, and in order to be effective, a tender had to deal with each
separate pursuer, because their claims were separate:  (Lord Justice Clerk Grant at page 79).
[17]
The case of McGillivray v Davidson 1993 SLT 693 was concerned with the question of
when a conclusion against several defenders jointly and severally, was competent, and
whether separate claims for damages by each pursuer required to be stated in separate
conclusions, or whether they could be stated separately in one conclusion.  The argument
which the court had to deal with for the second question, was that the conclusion should
either be a conclusion for payment to both pursuers, or in the form of a separate conclusion
for each pursuer (page 695C).  The Temporary Lord Ordinary's words at page 696 ought to
be seen in that context.  He was definitely not deciding and was not asked to decide that
pursuers who have suffered a loss jointly cannot sue for it jointly.
[18]
The defenders refer to Boulting v Elias 1990 SC 135, which looked at the competency
of an action where the two pursuers had raised an action against one defender;  on appeal it
was held that the averments disclosed two separate contracts of employment, one with each
pursuer on different terms, under which each was to be an employee of the defender in
regard to a particular business which she wished to set up;  (3) that each pursuer's claim had
to be founded upon a separate act, which was the defender's breach of the contract to which

7
he or she was the other party;  (4) that neither pursuer had a title to enforce the contract
which was entered into by the other;  and that neither had any interest in the other contract
in the legal sense of that word;  and, accordingly, (5) that the action was incompetent;
in short, different parties could not accumulate their actions in one libel, unless they had
connection with one another in the matters pursued for, or had been aggrieved by the same
act.  Two separate pursuers cannot conjoin in the same action in respect of separate and
independent grounds of debt, and he stressed, that this was to be seen not as a matter of
convenience, but as a rule.  It is recognised that two or more pursuers may join together in
the same action, each concluding for a separate sum of damages for himself while all found
on the same facts and circumstances as establishing the defender's liability:  Armstrong v
Paterson Bros 1935 SC 464, per Lord President Clyde at p 467.  In Buchan v Thomson 1976
SLT 42 at p 44, Lord Fraser acknowledged that this was competent, provided that two
conditions were satisfied, firstly, that the grounds of action by each pursuer were identical
and, secondly, that there was no material prejudice to the defenders by the pursuers
combining in one action.  (Lord Hope)
[19]
Flanagan v Dempster Moore & Co 1928 SC 308 related to a tender made in one sum to a
number of pursuers.  The court held that a tender was not effective, unless it offers a sum
appropriated to that pursuer.  The case arose because the tender as a whole, was not beaten,
but certain discrete offers made were beaten; the case was described (at p 314) as an
altogether exceptional case.  But the point made by the pursuers is that again, the case did
not assist in determination of whether such a single conclusion would be competent.
[20]
Finally the pursuers looked at Buchan v Thomson 1976 SLT 42;  in that case the court
looked at the procedural issues arising from the attempt to serve a third party notice on a
party already convened.  The defender appeared to rely on the wording at page 44 where

8
the Lord Ordinary said “…Although all the claims arise from the one wrong each pursuer
has a separate conclusion as he is bound to do….”  The pursuers submitted, that this
referred to the particular circumstances of the case, rather than stating a general principle.
[21]
It was submitted that, in essence, the issue to consider in relation to whether a
conclusion for the pursuers to sue jointly is appropriate, is whether there is a sufficient
nexus between the pursuers to allow them to be regarded as having a joint interest in the
remedy sought.
[22]
The pursuers were all parties to the same contract with the defender.  They all
suffered loss, as a result of the same failure and breach of contract.  They have all suffered
losses.  They have all suffered individual loss, in other words their own separate claims for
loss of society.  But the critical feature, was that they have also suffered losses for which they
are jointly and severally liable.  These circumstances clearly provide sufficient nexus in
order to allow the pursuers to sue jointly for recovery of the loss for which they have
suffered jointly and severally.  Indeed it is not clear that it could properly be done any other
way, where the joint and several liability exists for all of the pursuers and no payment has as
yet been made.  Each could be liable for the whole;  absent actual payment, the
apportionment cannot be done.  The issue identified in the case law was the indivisibility of
the loss.  A joint conclusion may be necessary if the remedy being pursued is indivisible.

Prescription
[23]
The pursuers submitted that there was no merit in the argument, that the two new
conclusions cannot be pursued because of prescription.  The claim after the proposed
amendment would still be a claim for the damage suffered by the pursuers in their
individual capacity.  In the closed record as it stands, each pursuer has averred that he or

9
she has suffered the loss of the relevant expenses.  The claims would still depend on a
breach of duty and breach of contract in the same manner, as relied on before amendment.
The obligation relied upon remained the obligation to make reparation for the averred
failure and breach of contract.  It is the obligation to make reparation, which the defenders
must show has prescribed.  The only change brought about by the amendment, is that part
of the damages for each pursuer is in the circumstances sought jointly with the other
pursuers.  The obligation under both contract and delict remains the same:  that is to make
reparation for the failure to lodge the summons for calling.  That obligation was founded on
by all pursuers in their individual capacity at the time of raising the current action.  Whether
those damages are sought separately or jointly is not relevant to the issue of prescription.
[24]
The original summons was clearly raised by the pursuers as individuals and it is that
capacity in which they continue to seek damages.  The original summons was clearly a
“relevant claim” for the purposes of the obligation to make reparation referred to above.
The question of whether some of the damage is suffered by each pursuer separately or
jointly with others is a matter which can be adjusted or amended.  Prescription has already
been interrupted for the liability to make reparation, which would allow recovery of
reparation for losses suffered by the pursuers in their individual capacity whether suffered
jointly or separately.

Defenders’ submissions
[25]
The defenders oppose this motion on the ground that the effect of the pursuers’
minute of amendment would be to introduce two new conclusions which are incompetent
and which seek to introduce incompetent claims into the action.

10
[26]
It was submitted, that the pursuers are six individuals who sue the defenders for
damages alleged to arise from breach of contract and/or negligence on the part of the
defenders.  (While the defenders purported not to understand, if this was one contract or six
different contracts, disputing that the pursuers “were all parties to the same contract with
the defenders.” submitting that the pursuers have no averments to support this assertion, or
that any contract that each had with the defenders were so linked that they stood or fell
together.  They do not have averments of fact to support a case whereby there existed
between themselves and the defenders a contract the terms of which were such that one
pursuer may enforce on behalf of any other pursuer contractual obligations owed by the
defenders to that other pursuer.  The pursuers confirmed that the basis of the action is as
averred in statement 8 of the condescendence, averring that it was a term:
“…express or implied of the Defender's contract to provide legal services to the
Pursuers that the Defender would provide the services to the standard of a solicitor
of suitable experience to carry out the instructions acting with ordinary skill and
ordinary care.  The Defenders also owed a concurrent duty of care to the Pursuers to
similar effect….”)

[27]
The defenders argue that as a matter of law, the claim of each pursuer in the action
calls for an individual and independent assessment of damages for that pursuer in the event
of them succeeding on liability, and accordingly requires an individual conclusion for each
such pursuer.  They referred to a number of authorities already referred to above to support
at proposition MacPhail’s:  Sheriff Court Practice, paragraph 4.45.
[28]
The defenders recognised that in certain circumstances multiple pursuers can sue in
one action.  As stated in MacPhail at paragraph 4.47, long standing case law provides that
surviving relatives, who wish to sue for damages arising from a death, must sue together in
one action, in order to enable the court to consider their claims as interrelated family claims.

11
[29]
The defenders submitted, however that, where it is competent for two or more
pursuers to sue in one action, there must be separate conclusions for each pursuer if
damages are sought.
[30]
The defenders looked at the pursuers’ reliance on the case of Tayside Contracts v
Geddes 2014 SLT 764 in support of their contention that it is competent (and relevant) for
them to sue in the one action with single conclusions for damages for the group as a whole.
[31]
Tayside Contracts was a case in which a joint committee formed by a combination of
three local authorities, sought damages in respect of an alleged breach of contract.  They
concluded for payment of a single sum.  The joint committee pursuer had been formed
pursuant to section 57(1) of the Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973, which provides:
“…For the purpose of discharging any functions of a local authority in pursuance of
arrangements made under section 56 of this Act… (b) two or more local authorities
may appoint a joint committee of those authorities….”

[32]
The defenders had moved for the action to be dismissed as incompetent on the basis
that the joint committee did not have an independent legal personality.  In holding that the
action was competent the Lord Ordinary stated (at page 767 L to 768 B):
“…The law has mechanisms for permitting voluntary associations, trade unions, and
trusts, none of which have a separate legal personality, to sue and be sued in respect
of debts owed to or by such bodies.  Such are sometimes called quasi-corporations,
for example, see Professor TB Smith’s Short Commentary at pp.272ff.
(Professor Smith speaks of the legislature intervening ‘for their regulation and
assistance’).  Why should the same not apply to direct labour trading organisations
such as Tayside Contracts?  And if so, what is wrong with the action being raised in
the name of the three constituent councils acting in combination for the recovery of a
single sum payable to the body with whom the defender contracted?...”

[33]
In their submissions, the pursuers narrated that any damages payable by the
defenders to the joint committee would thereafter be accounted for in accordance with the
financial arrangements agreed between the councils (page 768 E - F).  The court held that a
joint committee formed under section 57(1) of the 1973 Act, though not having its own legal

12
personality, could enter into contracts with third parties and carry out other acts in the
discharge of its functions, all as authorised by sections 56 and 57 of the 1973 Act.  That being
so the Lord Ordinary held (at page 768 J - L) that:
“…I see no difficulty with the three councils on that basis , seeking payment of a
single sum by way of damages, which will be payable to the joint committee and
thereafter accounted for in the agreed manner… I consider that all of this is implicit
in and authorised by the relevant statutory provisions….”

[34]
So, the defenders submit, the circumstances in Tayside Contracts could be
distinguished from the present case, because in that case, Parliament had legislated for the
pursuer to be formed as a single entity, and for it to trade with third parties as such;  there
clearly existed financial agreements between the constituent councils.  The circumstances of
that case were very far removed from those in the present case.  The defenders submitted,
that the incompetence of what the pursuers in the present case seek to do, was emphasised
by the fact that it was only by reason of legislation that the constituent councils who formed
the joint committee pursuer in Tayside Contracts were able to sue in one action with a single
conclusion.
[35]
The pursuers had made reference to the Stair Memorial Encyclopaedia on the Law of
Scotland, Volume 18, paragraph 29, but the passage relied upon appeared in a section of the
Encyclopaedia which was headed “Co-ownership” and all the cases referred to in it related
to co-ownership of property.  So, the defenders assert, none of the cases supported the
proposition, that multiple pursuers can conclude for a single sum by way of damages.
[36]
In identifying that, the issue to consider as to whether a conclusion for pursuers to
sue jointly is appropriate is whether there is sufficient nexus between the pursuers to allow
them to be regarded, as having a joint interest in the remedy sought.  They argued that here
the pursuers were all parties to the same contract with the defenders, and all suffered loss as

13
a result of the same failure and breach of contract, the pursuers approached the matter in the
wrong way.
[37]
But there was no authority for that proposition.  As stated in MacPhail’s:  Sheriff
Court Practice, 4th Edition at paragraph 4.45:
“…Two or more pursuers injured by the same wrong of the same defender and
claiming on the same grounds of action may join in one action, each claiming as an
individual, in a separate crave, a separate sum of damages.  They require however to
have been aggrieved by the same act of the defender or to have a community of
interest in the matter….”

[38]
The defenders returned to Boulting v Elias 1990 SC 135;  even where there exist
circumstances such that it is competent for two or more pursuers to sue in the one action,
they still require each to claim as an individual in a separate crave, a separate sum of
damages.  No authority to the contrary has been cited.
[39]
It was submitted ,that as the proposed new conclusions, sought to introduce
incompetent claims into the action that the amendment does not meet the requirements of
Rule of Court 24.1, and that the motion to amend, should be refused.  Reference was made to
MacPhail’s:  Sheriff Court Practice, 4th Edition Chapter 10 paragraph 10.05.

Prescription
[40]
The defenders submitted, that the proposed amendment related to an alleged
obligation to pay to a group of persons (the pursuers) a single sum of money in respect of
damages said to be owed to the group as a single body.  The pursuers in the unamended
action do not sue as a single body.  They sue as individuals, each for their own alleged loss.
If the pursuers require to sue as a group for a single sum in order to make good their claims
in respect of each of the alleged losses to which proposed new conclusions 1 and 2 relate, the
proposed new claims are made by the pursuers as a group rather than as individuals.

14
Accordingly, if the amendment were given effect to the pursuers, in respect of each of
proposed new conclusions 1 and 2, they would be suing in respect of those conclusions in a
different capacity from that in which they sue in the existing action.  Any right that the
pursuers may have had to sue as a single body has prescribed in terms of section 6 of the
David Johnston, Prescription and limitation  of Actions, 2nd Edition;  Tecjet Limited v Keir
Construction Limited [2024], SLT 1 168;  Dunlop v McGowans 1980 SC (HL) 73.
[41]
An obligation owed to a group qua group, is a different obligation from that owed to
an individual, as an individual.  In the unamended pleadings, each of the pursuers founds
on obligations said to be owed to each of them as individuals.  By the minute of amendment
the pursuers sue in respect of an obligation allegedly owed to a group rather than to
individuals.  That alleged obligation owed to the group qua group, now founded on by the
pursuers has prescribed.
[42]
An amendment which seeks to introduce an obligation that has prescribed does not
meet the requirements of Rule of Court 24.1.  In any event, as stated in David Johnston on
Prescription and Limitation 32nd Edition at paragraph 22.21 on page 415:
“…allowing pleadings relating to a non-existent (because prescribed) obligation to
enter the record does not affect the fact that there is still no obligation.  In clear cases
therefore, it seems that the Court should refuse such amendments at the time the
motion is made either for receipt of the minute of amendment or for amendment in
terms of the minute of amendment….”

[43]
For this further reason also, it is submitted, that the motion to amend should be
refused.

Basis for decision
[44]
It is argued, that it is not competent to have one conclusion for all pursuers in
relation to the any element of the damages claimed.  It is said that neither authority nor

15
textbook supports the pursuers’ proposition;  I do not regard the absence of authority as
determinative;  such circumstances will be rare, but are not excluded simply by reason of the
rarity;  it is function of a smaller jurisdiction, that the law may develop slowly, as there are
limited opportunities for the law to develop.
[45]
The pursuers had made reference to the Stair Memorial Encyclopaedia on the Law of
Scotland, Volume 18, paragraph 29;  the passage relied upon appeared in a section of the
Encyclopaedia which was headed “Co-ownership” and all the cases referred to in related to
co-ownership of property.  So, the defenders assert, none of the cases supported the
proposition that multiple pursuers can conclude for a single sum by way of damages;  but
such a decision depends on the nature of the damages.
[46]
The defenders rely on the passage in MacPhail Chapter 4.45, quoted at para [37] to
support their position.
[47]
That passage deals with the conventional action, where each pursuer will have a
different, sometimes a very different, and discrete claim for injury loss or damage;  in that
context the need for separate self-contained claims is intelligible, both in principle and logic.
But I do not take that passage to necessarily restrict the terms of any crave or conclusion,
depending on the particular circumstances of the case.
[48]
The defenders referred for support for the proposition in MacPhail to the case of
Boulting v Elias submitting, that this case made clear that, even where there existed
circumstances such that it is competent for two or more pursuers to sue in the one action,
each pursuer still requires to claim, as an individual, in a separate conclusion, a separate
sum of damages.  But the circumstances in Boulting were of two pursuers seeking to sue on
the basis of two discrete contracts;  and the loss or damages claimed was different and
discrete for each pursuer.  It is not relevant to the circumstances in respect of this case.

16
The decision reiterated that different parties could not “…accumulate their actions in one
libel…” unless they had connection with one another in the matters pursued for, or had been
aggrieved by the same act ”…. Two separate pursuers cannot conjoin in the same action in
respect of separate and independent grounds of debt;…”:  that can hardly be regarded as
controversial.
[49]
It is recognised, that two or more pursuers may join together in the same action, each
concluding for a separate sum of damages for himself while all found on the same facts and
circumstances as establishing the defender's liability:  (Armstrong v Paterson Bros 1935
SC 464, per Lord President Clyde at p 467).
[50]
That rule is so well established as to not require any tracing of its development.
The question for this court, is whether that vehicle, for having more than one pursuer claim
in the same action for losses arising out of the same wrong, provides a bar to a single
conclusion in relation to a loss sustained by the pursuers as a group, distinct from the
individual losses alleged to have been sustained.
[51]
It is helpful to trace the development of the authorities to which I was referred;  the
starting point is Lawson v Leith and Newcastle Steam Packet Company (1850) 13 D 175;  that case
dealt with a part owner suing for losses after the destruction of a vessel;  the case was
concerned with the title to sue of the part owner;  the court held that a part owner can sue;
the court’s approach is worth recording.
[52]
The Lord Justice Clerk (Hope) said at p 178:
“…The defenders plead, that the pursuer has no title to sue the action, on the ground
that part-owners cannot sue separately.  I think it important, at the outset, to state,
that while this was pleaded as a general rule, yet Mr Marshall candidly admitted that
it could not be universal—for he admitted, that if one owner had discharged his
claim, the other would have a title to sue such an action.  Now, such an exception
must rest on the injustice which would be done if the rule were of absolute and
peremptory application in all such cases.  And equally I hold, that whenever the rule

17
contended for, if it really exists, would operate unjustly, it cannot obtain.  The fact on
which this summons is founded, is the destruction of the property of which there
were part-owners, and, by that destruction, the sort of bond which united them
together is entirely destroyed in regard to this claim - although it might have
subsisted in regard to any contract or adventure, respecting the vessel, on which any
claim still existed….”

[53]
Lord Cockburn said at p 182:
“…Suppose there had been sixty-four owners, and that sixty-three of them concurred
in the action, but that one refused, could the plea of want of title be maintained in
such a case? The mind would revolt from such a judgment, as inconsistent with
justice and common sense….”

[54]
Each emphasises, in considering the procedural route to be taken, that there is a role
for justice and common sense.  That must be right – in that procedure should be the servant
not the master.
[55]
Harkes v Mowat (1862) 24 D 701 at page 703 was cited as authority for the proposition
that combined claims require separate conclusions for each pursuer;  the Lord Justice Clerk
(Lord Glencorse) said (emphasis added):
“…The other point is one of considerable importance.  I think the two pursuers are
entitled to issues under this summons, for this reason, that it concludes for damages
to each separately arising out of one wrong.  Now the fact of the wrong being single
is a justification of the two claims being in one libel;  but the fact that the injury of
each pursuer is separate, makes it necessary that the conclusions should apply to
each pursuer separately, as those of this summons do.  I think this view is supported
by the important case of Revey, 11th March 1841 (3 D. 888).  Though the Inner-House
did not decide this point, it was disposed of by Lord Fullerton.  There is in the
present summons only one conclusion, but the claims of damages are separately
stated.  I see no objection to this;  but it is clear that the pursuers must take separate
issues….”

[56]
Again, the decision identifies as the critical point, the fact that the injury of each
pursuer is separate, making a separate conclusion necessary.  Again, that accords with
common sense, but says nothing about the situation where there is an indivisible loss
sustained.

18
[57]
Flanagan v Dempster Moore & co Ltd 1928 SC 308 dealt with a tender which offered a
single sum, which was then apportioned with a particular sum to each pursuer.  The issue
arose about whether it was a proper tender;  the court held that on the construction of the
tender adopted by the Lord Ordinary, and accepted by the parties, that it was invalid;  in a
case with a plurality of pursuers, it was incompetent to tender a lump sum (although the
Inner House appear to have viewed the tender as being valid because of the apportionment,
but proceeded in the basis of the parties agreed construction).
[58]
But the Inner House observations included the following at p 312 where the
Lord President Clyde said:
“…[It] sic is not, in my opinion, possible to make a valid lump-sum tender to a
plurality of pursuers in such an action.  The pursuers do not conclude for a lump
sum which they may allocate or dispute about among themselves;  on the contrary,
each pursuer claims the specific amount of compensation to which he conceives
himself to be entitled in respect of the loss of solace and support which he
individually has suffered through the death of husband or wife, father or mother,
son or daughter, as the case may be….”

[59]
That seems to anticipate the possibility of the pursuers, in particular circumstances
concluding for a lump sum.  As we shall see, that logic is followed in Tayside, where in the
particular circumstances the pursers did conclude for a lump sum.
[60]
McNeil v NCB 1966 SC 72 was again concerned with the question of whether a tender
lodged by defenders of a single sum (in respect of a mother and daughter suing in one
action, but with separate conclusions) was an effective tender.  In that case, it was confirmed
that a tender for a single sum to cover the individual claims of relatives was not an effective
tender.  The claims were separate and, in order to be effective, a tender had to deal with each
separate pursuer, because their claims were separate:  that is sound in logic and consistent
with the decision in Flanagan.  But again, it is of no assistance in informing the court about
the competence of a single conclusion in relation to an indivisible loss.

19
[61]
The defenders had placed reliance on Buchan v Thomson and in particular the
observation at p 44 where Lord Fraser said “…Although all the claims arise from the one
wrong, each pursuer has a separate conclusion, as he is bound to do….”  Reference was
made to Harkes as authority for that proposition.
[62]
Lord Fraser went on to say at pp 44/45:
“…Although all the claims will normally be tried together, each will be adjudicated
upon separately, by a separate issue in the case of a jury trial, or after separate
consideration by the judge at a proof.  It is possible that a defence might be sustained
against one pursuer and not against another, for example, a defence of volenti non fit
injuria might be sustained against only one pursuer, or a defence that one pursuer
had discharged his claim might be sustained against him but not against the others.
Having regard to all these points of separation between the claims, counsel for the
pursuers in my opinion was well founded in saying that where several pursuers join
in a single process, as they have done in the present case, the process is used by them
as a convenient procedure to house a number of separate claims which are, from
many points of view, properly regarded as separate actions….”

[63]
The decision reflected the various points of separation which existed;  the procedure
was considered to be a convenient vehicle for all claims, although properly regarded as
separate actions.  Again, it seems to me that the wording used does not exclude the
possibility of an indivisible or inseparable claim by a multitude of pursuers being sought in
one conclusion.
[64]
The case leading up to Tayside, does not preclude or prohibit a single conclusion;
Tayside involved a joint committee of three local authorities who pooled resources to
purchase aggregates.  A dispute  arose;  using the vehicle of the joint committee, the local
authorities sued for damages.  The defenders sought to challenge the pursuers title to sue.
In repelling the defenders’ challenge, the Lord Ordinary said:
“…[28] The result is that Tayside Contracts, though not having its own legal
personality, can enter into contracts with third parties and carry out other acts in
discharge of its functions, all as authorised by ss.56 and 57 of the 1973 Act.  In these
circumstances it makes sense that any litigation of the present kind should be framed
in the name of the constituent councils acting together under the designation of

20
Tayside Contracts.  I see no difficulty with the three councils, on that basis, seeking
payment of a single sum by way of damages, which will be payable to the joint
committee and thereafter accounted for in the agreed manner.  No individual council
has any right to an identifiable share or part of the damages, but rather the whole
sum is payable to the joint committee as the contracting party.  I consider that all of
this is implicit in and authorised by the relevant statutory provisions.  It may be that
Tayside Contracts can be thought of as ‘a legal entity’ similar to that described by
Lord Keith of Avonholm in the context of a trade union in Bonsor v Musicians Union
at [1956] A.C., pp.150ff.  That said, if the suit was at the hand of the contracting third
party, I doubt if the claim would be constrained to exclude diligence against the
property of the member councils….”

[65]
I take from this, that there are circumstances in which a joint claim may be made;  the
circumstance in which such a joint conclusion may be apt will be limited.  In the instant case,
the pursuers seek payment of a single sum by way of damages, which relates to the sums
due to the defenders from the earlier proceedings and a single sum representing sums due
to their solicitors in relation to the costs incurred.  Effectively no individual pursuer has any
right to an identifiable share or part of the damages covered by these conclusions, but rather
the whole sum is payable to defray the losses sustained.
[66]
I do not regard Tayside Contracts as determining, that a sine qua non of such a
conclusion must be the existence of a statutory basis.  In Tayside Contracts, the legislative
foundation allowed the court to identify, that the nature of the claim could be articulated
through one conclusion.  The law accordingly recognises that in certain circumstances,
pursuers can sue for sums due in one conclusion if there is a unity in doing so.
[67]
I did consider whether the difficulties which might arise in tendering, provide a bar
to the conclusion to be added.  The defenders pointed to authorities involving tenders,
arguing that these showed, that a joint conclusion was precluded (McNeil v NCB, Flanagan v
Moore);  in fact these are authorities to the effect that the tender must match the
conclusion(s), that a single tender to a number of pursuers must break down the sums in
accordance with the separate conclusions.  I consider that tender procedure is more flexible

21
than contended for.  The days in which a tender has to be explicit, unqualified and
unconditional are, I consider, gone;  the pragmatism of the Lord Ordinary in Ferguson v
McLennan Salmon Co Limited 1990 SC 45 is to be preferred;  so long as a tender is in clear and
unambiguous terms which it is open to the other side to accept, it will be a valid tender.
Such a tender could be constructed, whatever the terms of the conclusions.
[68]
In this case, the pursers find themselves (through no fault of their own, on one view)
facing payment of a sum of expenses;  that sum has not been broken down to apply a
particular sum to each pursuer.  The court in the earlier action saw fit to group the pursuers
together and to make an order against them as one group for the purposes of an award of
expenses,  This was intelligible and appropriate.  Their interest and liability were indivisible
in that context.  How can it not be appropriate to allow the same group to now seek recover
the same sum as part of a larger claim against the defenders who, the pursuers say, were
responsible for that loss?
[69]
The claims made by the pursuers in relation to the new conclusions are not some
contrived device or some opportunistic claim.  It is in relation to the first new conclusion, a
direct consequence of this court making an award against the pursuers as a group, they
having been unsuccessful in an action which was raised as a result of the failure to raise
proceedings timeously.  The pursuers are not casting about for some mechanism to increase
the scope of an award of damages;  they are rather seeking that the court recognise a
practical and appropriate mechanism for a loss the pursuers claim to have already
sustained.
[70]
The critical feature is, that the pursuers aver that they have suffered losses for which
they are jointly and severally liable.  These circumstances clearly provide sufficient nexus to
allow the pursuers to sue jointly for recovery of the loss which they have suffered jointly

22
and severally.  Indeed it is not clear that it could properly be done any other way, where the
joint and several liability exists for all of the pursuers and no payment has as yet been made.
Each could be liable for the whole;  absent actual payment, the apportionment cannot be
done.  Their claim in relation to the elements of the claim contained in the new conclusions
which the pursuers seek to add are indivisible and inseparable.
[71]
If the defenders were correct about their approach, it would be impossible for the
pursuers ever to recover their expenses unless they embarked upon some artificial, and on
the face of it, pointless attribution of parts of the expenses to each pursuer.  The Law of
Scotland is, I suggest, flexible enough to recognise, that in the particular circumstances of
this case, the pursuers’ approach is the appropriate route to recover the sums.  (Ferguson v
McLennan Salmon Co Ltd 1990 SC 45), is a good example of the inherent flexibility and the
need for evolution and development).  The alternative is an unattractive inflexibility, where
a claim may founder entirely on procedural grounds, because of an inability to provide
some precise breakdown or pro rata analysis.  Accordingly, I find that the minute of
amendment provides for a remedy which is both competent and relevant.

Prescription
[72]
I can deal with the matter briefly.  The issue of prescription arises not from the
capacity in which parties sue, but whether a relevant claim has been made.  It is recognised
that brief even irrelevant actions can be sufficient to be a relevant claim.  There is no change
to the nature of the case, the allegations of negligence etc remain the same - as was said in
MacPhail:
“…10.36
The court, in considering whether to exercise its discretion to allow
amendment, has regard to the object of the relevant statutory provision as to
time-bar.  In Greenhorn v J. Smart (Contractors) Ltd it was observed that if the

23
pursuer’s case as amended were allowed to proceed the defenders would be
deprived of the protection which they were intended to enjoy under the relevant
provision, the clear policy of which was to protect defenders against stale claims
which after the passage of time would be difficult to investigate and resist.  On the
other hand, an action in relation to a claim to which section 6(1) of the Prescription
and Limitation (Scotland) Act 1973 applies may be extensively amended after the
expiry of the five-year period, so long as the obligation remains the same, its
expression or the grounds for it may be altered…

…10.37
The sum sued for may be increased, and any necessary averments to
support the new figure added, by amendment after the expiry of a timelimit.  If the
amendment is one which is necessary for determining in the existing action the real
question in controversy between the parties, the question whether it should be
allowed is a matter for the discretion of the court in all the circumstances of the
particular case.  If objection is to be taken to an amendment on the ground of time-
bar and a plea is set out to this effect in the answers, the appropriate way of dealing
with the matter is for the court to decide, as a matter of discretion, whether or not to
allow the amendment, including the allegedly time-barred averments, at the time
when it is dealing with the motion to amend the record….”

[73]
The basis for the argument, is that the pursuers are seeking this sum as a group,
distinguishing them from the conclusions sought as individuals, so they are thereby
transformed from  one legal entity into another;  I do not agree.  The basis of the case
remains identical;  the only charge is in the vehicle of recovery of a discrete part of the claim,
one in which the claims of the pursuers are indivisible or inseparable.
[74]
There is no merit in the prescription argument;  that matter remains for the discretion
of the court and I exercise it in favour of the pursuers.
[75]
Accordingly I allow the minute of amendment of the pursuers to be received and
allow the closed record to be opened up and amended in terms of the minute of amendment
and answers.  The pursuers have conceded the expenses of the amendment procedure, but
not those relating to the argument over competency.  I will accordingly reserve these
expenses meantime.

title: Iain Gray against RW Motor Company Limited
text:
SHERIFF APPEAL COURT
[2026] SAC (Civ) 43
DNF-SG325-25
Sheriff Principal Gillian A Wade KC

STATEMENT OF REASONS
delivered by SHERIFF PRINCIPAL GILLIAN A WADE KC
in the appeal in the cause
IAIN GRAY
Claimant and Appellant
against
RW MOTOR COMPANY LIMITED
Respondent and Respondent
Claimant and Appellant:  Party
Respondent and Respondent:  Absent
3 July 2026
[1]
Although this appeal arises form a very low value simple procedure claim it raises a
number of important matters in relation to the application of The Consumer Contracts
(Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 which are worthy of
clarification.
[2]
The appeal is taken against the decision of the sheriff at Dunfermline dated 3 October
2025 to dismiss the appellant’s simple procedure claim ex proprio motu following a case
management discussion and on consideration of the documentary productions which he
had before him.

2

[3]
The appellant sought an order for payment against the respondent in the sum
of £99.00 which he had paid by way of a deposit to reserve a Citroen C3 car.  The deposit
was paid online via the PayPal service on 15 December 2024 to reserve the car for a period of
5 days as part of a contract to purchase the vehicle.  On 22 December 2024, the appellant
advised the respondent that he no longer wished to purchase the car, having become aware
that the road tax for the vehicle was higher than advertised.  The appellant thereafter asked
for the deposit to be refunded and the respondent refused.
[4]
The appellant raised a simple procedure claim.  His initial claim form was predicated
on two grounds:  (i) firstly, that the deposit was described as fully refundable via the
respondent’s website and there were no other terms and conditions (“the refundable
ground”) (ii) secondly, that the respondent misrepresented the road tax payable for the
vehicle at the point the deposit was paid as the respondent advised the road tax payable
was £190 whereas it was £345 per annum (“the misrepresentation ground”).
[5]
The respondent’s position was:  (i) firstly, that the contract was entered into on
15 December 2024 and per the terms and conditions was governed by the law of England
and Wales and, separately, that the courts in England and Wales had exclusive jurisdiction
(ii) secondly, that the terms and conditions of the contract, which applied at the time of
paying the deposit, provided that the deposit was non-refundable (iii) thirdly, there was no
misdescription of the road tax position by the respondent and the road tax payable was £190
per annum and not £345 per annum (iv) the respondent incurred costs or losses as a result of
holding the vehicle for a period of 7 days.
[6]
The respondent produced the relevant terms and conditions dated March 2024
(the “Terms”).  The Terms included the following clauses:

3

“1.4. ‘Goods’ refers to any vehicle, including cars, vans, motorcycles, or accessories,
sold by the Dealer to the Customer.
1.5. ‘Purchase Price’ refers to the agreed price for the Goods as specified in the
Order.
1.6. ‘Order’ refers to the contract or order form for the purchase of the Goods.

2.
Whole Contract
2.1. These Terms and Conditions, together with the Order, form the entire contract
between the Dealer and the Customer.  They may only be varied by written
agreement signed by both parties.

3.
Vehicle Condition and Statutory Rights
3.1. All vehicles are supplied as roadworthy at the time of delivery, in accordance
with the Sale of Goods Act 1979 (as amended) and the Consumer Rights
Act 2015 for Consumer sales.

5.
Payment and Delivery
5.1. The Customer shall pay the Purchase Price in full in cleared funds (by bank
transfer or debit card) before or upon delivery, unless otherwise agreed in
writing by an authorised representative of the Dealer.
5.2. A non-refundable deposit of £99 (for online reservations) or £350 (for telephone
reservations) is required to secure the vehicle for a period of 5 days.  This
deposit will only be refunded if the vehicle is found not to be as described at
the time of inspection or delivery.

8.
Consumer Rights and Cancellation
8.1. For Consumer sales conducted off-premises or at a distance (e.g., online or by
telephone), the Customer has a 14-day cancellation period starting from the
day they take physical possession of the Goods, as per The Consumer
Contracts Regulations 2013.
8.2. To cancel, the Customer must notify the Dealer in writing (e.g., by email or
post to the Dealer).  The Customer is responsible for returning the Goods
within 14 days of cancellation at their own cost, unless the Dealer fails to
inform them of this responsibility.

13.
Governing Law
13.1. This contract is governed by the laws of England and Wales. Any disputes will
be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of England and Wales.”

[7]
In light of these Terms, at the initial case management discussion, the sheriff ordered
the appellant to lodge the documentary evidence to support his position that the deposit
was refundable and that the respondent had misstated the position regarding the road tax
payable for the vehicle.  In response to that order, the appellant lodged five documents

4

entitled “C1” to “C5”.  Document C3 is a screenshot from the respondent’s website which
provides:  “Reserve this Peugeot 2008 for only £99…A £99 fully refundable deposit reserves
this car for up to 5 days”.
[8]
At the end of document C3 there is a “tick-box” which requires to be ticked to accept
the “terms”.  Document C2 bears to be a letter from the respondent to the appellant which
provides as follows:
“Before paying the holding fee a tick box window pops up and doesn’t allow you to
male [sic] a payment unless the terms are agreed with.  The contents of the tick box
window clearly states that the holding fee will reserve the vehicle for 5 days.

As a reference for you and ill attach it wit [sic] this document, I have just taken a
screenshot from the websites [sic] payment link confirming what I’ve mentioned
above.  Its [sic] referenced to a different vehicle…the payment link tick box is auto
generated and the exact same for every vehicle”.

[9]
The appellant produced written submissions in a document C5 in which he stated:
“The only terms that I agreed to are uploaded as Evidence, Reference C-3.  Any other
terms, as uploaded by the Respondent, were added to their website after I
commenced Court proceedings.  The Respondent’s document, entitled Terms and
Conditions of Sale for RW Motor Co, and conveniently dated March 2024, was not on
their website when I paid the fully refundable deposit.  This document was
subsequently added to their website and is not dated.”

Sheriff’s judgment
[10]
The sheriff dismissed the appellant’s claim ex proprio motu in accordance with simple
procedure rule 1.8(11), which provides:  “If a claim, or part of a claim, obviously has no real
prospect of success, the sheriff may dismiss the claim or that part of it at any time.”
[11]
As regards the refundability ground, and the conflict between the Terms (upon
which the respondent relied) and the tick box form on the respondent’s website (upon which
the appellant relied), the sheriff preferred the respondent’s position for two reasons.  Firstly,
document C3 related to a different vehicle entirely and had presumably been raised by the

5

appellant to demonstrate what the equivalent form looked like for the vehicle when he paid
his deposit.  Secondly, that the appellant’s position that the Terms did not exist and were not
available to him when paying the deposit was implausible as it would require the
respondent to have produced and uploaded the Terms in response to a claim for £99.
As such, in accordance with the Terms, the party’s contract was clear and the deposit was
non-refundable per Clause 5.2.  If document C3 or something similar applied at the point the
appellant paid the deposit, it must be read in light of the Terms including Clause 5.2.
[12]
As regards the misrepresentation ground, the sheriff was not satisfied the
respondent had any evidence of a misrepresentation having been made.

Grounds of appeal
[13]
The appellant relies upon four grounds of appeal:
1.
that the sheriff erred in law in failing to apply the Consumer Contracts
(Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 (“the
2013 Regulations”);
2.
that the sheriff erred in law in misinterpreting the contractual term that the
deposit was fully refundable as the ordinary meaning of that term was clear
under reference to Arnold v Briton [2015] UKSC 36;
3.
that the sheriff erred in law as a result of a procedural irregularity in failing to
notice that the person appearing on behalf of the respondent at the two
hearings was different yet claimed to be the same person;
4.
the sheriff erred in law in failing to take into account the respondent’s
misrepresentation of the road tax position in relation to the vehicle.

6

[14]
In the appeal report, the sheriff poses four questions for the opinion of this court:
1.
Does the court have jurisdiction to deal with the case standing the prorogation
clause in the parties’ contract.
2.
Was the transaction covered by the 2013 Regulations and did the appellant
have a right to cancel within 14 days.
3.
Was I right to dismiss the claim on the basis that in terms of rule 1.8(11) as the
claim obviously has no real prospect of success.
4.
Was I right in holding that the claimant had not produced evidence that the
vehicle was sold subject to a description of having a road tax of £190 and
therefore that section 11 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 had not been
breached.
I shall deal with each in turn.

Jurisdiction
[15]
Jurisdiction is pars judicis and determines whether this court is properly seized of the
remaining questions.  The sheriff concluded that he had jurisdiction as a result of
paragraph 3(3) of Schedule 8 to the Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982 (“the
1982 Act”).  For the most part, the rules for jurisdiction in relation to Scotland are found in
Schedule 8 to the 1982 Act read with section 20 of the 1982 Act.  However, this is subject to
any specific provision made in Part II of the 1982 Act.  Specific provision is made in
section 16 (read with Schedule 4) for the allocation of jurisdiction as between the courts in
the three jurisdictions of the United Kingdom.  Moreover, sections 15A to 15E of the
1982 Act provide specific provision in relation to the allocation of jurisdiction concerning

7

inter alia consumer contracts.  These provisions are relevant particularly in light of the
respondent’s plea of no jurisdiction.
[16]
Sections 15A to 15E of the 1982 Act were inserted by the Civil Jurisdiction and
Judgments (Amendment) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (the “2019 Regulations”).
In accordance with sections 15A to 15E of the 1982 Act, specific provision is made in relation
to establishing jurisdiction for disputes concerning certain consumer contracts.  These rules
operate to determine jurisdiction as between different parts of the UK and, separately, where
the dispute has an international connection (paragraph 2.6 of the Explanatory Memorandum
to the 2019 Regulations;  Macphail’s Sheriff Court Practice (4th Edition), Chapters 3.86 - 3.91).
[17]
In terms of section 15A of the 1982 Act, the rules apply where the subject-matter of
the proceedings and the nature of the proceedings fall within the scope of Article 1 of
Council Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 (“the Regulation”) (as it applied immediately
before IP completion day).  Section 15A(2) defines the scope of application of section 15B (for
consumers) to proceedings whose “subject matter” and “nature” are within the scope of the
Regulation as determined by Article 1 of the Regulation.  Applying these principles, the
contract entered into between the parties falls within the subject matter of Article 1 of the
Regulation as the action concerns civil and commercial matters and is not an excluded action
within the terms of the Regulation.
[18]
In turn, section 15E(1) defines “consumer” and the “consumer contracts” to which
the jurisdictional protection is afforded using the same language as Article 17 of the
Regulation (Soleymani v Nifty Gateway LLC [2022] EWCA Civ 1297, per Popplewell LJ at
paras [55] - [57]).  The appellant is clearly a consumer in this context within the meaning of
section 15E(1).  In this context, a “consumer contract” means a contract concluded with a
person who pursues commercial activities and by any means directs such activities to the

8

part of the UK where the consumer is domiciled.  In assessing whether a trader has directed
their activities to another part of the UK, the court should consider that (i) there is no need
for a specific invitation to the consumer (ii) whether activities are “directed” to a particular
jurisdiction requires more than mere accessibility of a website (iii) evidence of an intention
to solicit custom from another part of the UK will indicate that the activities have been
directed to that part of the UK and (iv) there is no need to show subjective intention of the
trader and the question is whether, if viewed objectively from the perspective of the average
consumer, a trader’s internet activity was targeted at consumers in other parts of the UK
(Bitar v Banque Libano-Francaise SAL [2021] EWHC 2787 (QB), at paras [12] - [14], [17] - [21],
[25] - [27]).
[19]
In light of the evidence available, including the appellant’s position, the respondent’s
written submissions and extracts from the respondent’s website, it is clear that, viewed
objectively from the perspective of the average consumer, the respondent’s website seeks to
solicit customers from throughout the UK.  As such, this dispute concerns a consumer
contract to which sections 15A to 15E of the 1982 Act apply.
[20]
The respondent sought to rely on standing Clause 13.1 of the Terms which provides
that the courts of England and Wales have exclusive jurisdiction.  However Clause 13.1 can
have no effect.  Section 15B(2)(a) entitles the appellant to bring a claim in the courts for the
place where he is domiciled.  The parties can only contract out of that rule after the dispute
has arisen and if other conditions are met per section 15B(6)(a).  Agreements which confer
exclusion jurisdiction (such as Clause 13 of the Terms) have no legal force if they are
contrary to section 15B(6).
[21]
Accordingly Clause 13 is of no legal effect and this court has jurisdiction as a result of
section 15B(2)(b) of the 1982 Act (as opposed to Schedule 8 to the 1982 Act as relied upon by

9

the sheriff).  Although the sheriff was right to conclude that the court had jurisdiction he
said so for the wrong reasons.  The sheriff’s first question falls to be answered in the
affirmative.
[22]
Although the respondent also raised an issue regarding the applicable law there is no
question posed by the sheriff in this regard and neither party has sought to insist upon it.
Accordingly I have not addressed the matter further.

The application of the 2013 Regulations
[23]
At first instance the sheriff did not consider these Regulations on the basis that they
had not been brought to his attention.  However, during adjustment of the appeal report,
there was a dispute about this which is recorded in the report.  Whilst it is competent to
raise a new point on appeal that was not raised before the sheriff (Varney (Scotland) Ltd v
Lanark Town Council 1974 SC 245, per LJC Wheatley at 249) there must be a corresponding
basis in the pleadings for a party to advance such a case.  Following sundry procedure
during the course of this appeal, the appellant made an additional orders application to
amend his claim form to introduce a claim anent the 2013 Regulations.  This was not
opposed as both parties wished clarification as to the legal position in relation to the
applicability of the Regulations.
[24]
These Regulations provide:
“4.
In these Regulations—
‘consumer’ means an individual acting for purposes which are wholly or mainly
outside that individual's trade, business, craft or profession;
‘trader’ means a person acting for purposes relating to that person's trade, business,
craft or profession, whether acting personally or through another person acting in
the trader's name or on the trader's behalf.”

“5.
In these Regulations—
‘business premises’ in relation to a trader means—

10

(a)
any immovable retail premises where the activity of the trader is carried out
on a permanent basis…
‘distance contract’ means a contract concluded between a trader and a consumer
under an organised distance sales or service-provision scheme without the
simultaneous physical presence of the trader and the consumer, with the exclusive
use of one or more means of distance communication up to and including the time at
which the contract is concluded…
‘goods’ means any tangible moveable items, but that includes water, gas and
electricity if and only if they are put up for sale in a limited volume or a set quantity;
‘sales contract’ means a contract under which a trader transfers or agrees to transfer
the ownership of goods to a consumer and the consumer pays or agrees to pay the
price, including any contract that has both goods and services as its object”

“Making information etc available to a consumer
8.
For the purposes of this Part, something is made available to a consumer only if
the consumer can reasonably be expected to know how to access it.”

“Information to be provided before making a distance contract
13.—(1)  Before the consumer is bound by a distance contract, the trader—
(a)
must give or make available to the consumer the information listed in
Schedule 2 in a clear and comprehensible manner, and in a way
appropriate to the means of distance communication used, and
(b)
if a right to cancel exists, must give or make available to the consumer
a cancellation form as set out in part B of Schedule 3.”

“Requirements for distance contracts concluded by electronic means
14.—(1)
This regulation applies where a distance contract is concluded by
electronic means.
(2)
If the contract places the consumer under an obligation to pay, the trader
must make the consumer aware in a clear and prominent manner, and
directly before the consumer places the order, of the information listed in
paragraphs (a), (f), (g), (h), (s) and (t) of Schedule 2.
(3)
The trader must ensure that the consumer, when placing the order,
explicitly acknowledges that the order implies an obligation to pay.
(4)
If placing an order entails activating a button or a similar function, the
trader must ensure that the button or similar function is labelled in an
easily legible manner only with the words ‘order with obligation to pay’
or a corresponding unambiguous formulation indicating that placing the
order entails an obligation to pay the trader.
(5)
If the trader has not complied with paragraphs (3) and (4), the consumer
is not bound by the contract or order.”

“Right to cancel
29.—(1)
The consumer may cancel a distance or off-premises contract at any time
in the cancellation period without giving any reason, and without
incurring any liability…

11

(2)
The cancellation period begins when the contract is entered into and ends
in accordance with regulation 30 or 31.”

“Normal cancellation period
30.—(1)
The cancellation period ends as follows, unless regulation 31 applies…
(3)
If the contract is a sales contract and none of paragraphs (4) to (6) applies,
the cancellation period ends at the end of 14 days after the day on which
the goods come into the physical possession of—
(a)
the consumer, or
(b)
a person, other than the carrier, identified by the consumer to take
possession of them.

Effect of withdrawal or cancellation
33.—(1)
If a contract is cancelled under regulation 29(1)—
(a)
the cancellation ends the obligations of the parties to perform the
contract, and
(b)
regulations 34 to 38 apply.

Reimbursement by trader in the event of withdrawal or cancellation
34.—(1)
The trader must reimburse all payments, other than payments for
delivery, received from the consumer, subject to paragraph (10)…
(9)
If (in the case of a sales contract) the value of the goods is diminished by
any amount as a result of handling of the goods by the consumer beyond
what is necessary to establish the nature, characteristics and functioning
of the goods, the trader may recover that amount from the consumer, up
to the contract price.
(10) An amount that may be recovered under paragraph (9)—
(a)
may be deducted from the amount to be reimbursed under
paragraph (1);
(b)
otherwise, must be paid by the consumer to the trader.
(11) Paragraph (9) does not apply if the trader has failed to provide the
consumer with the information on the right to cancel required by
paragraph (l) of Schedule 2, in accordance with Part 2…
(13) Where the provisions of this regulation apply to cancellation of a
contract, the contract is to be treated as including those provisions as
terms.”

[25]
The contract which forms the subject matter of this appeal is between a consumer
and a trader within the meaning of Regulation 4 of the 2013 Regulations.  The contract was
not concluded at any business premises of the respondent and it was concluded by means of
distance communication, namely the respondent’s website.  On the respondent’s own
admission, this is a sales contract for the sale of the vehicle and the deposit was part of the

12

contract to purchase rather than a reservation fee forming part of a different contract
because (i) the deposit paid was part of the appellant’s “Order” of the vehicle within the
meaning of Clause 1.6 of the Terms (ii) Clause 2 of the Terms provides that there is only one
contract consisting of the Order and the Terms (iii) Clause 5.2 of the Terms clearly identifies
this as a deposit forming part of the overall contract to purchase (iv) the appellant was
bound by contract to purchase the vehicle at the point of paying the deposit (v) the ordinary
meaning of the word “deposit” in this context is an amount of money you pay as part of a
total sum due or which will be returned if the agreed arrangement is completed (vi) this was
not merely a holding fee but part of the overall contract of purchase which was concluded at
the same time which is evidenced by the deposit only being refundable in the event that the
vehicle was found not to be as described at the time of inspection or delivery
(vii) document C3 refers to the vehicle being prepared for delivery (ie conclusion of the
respondent’s obligations under the contract).  Read in this light, the deposit formed part of
the contract to purchase without the appellant ever having seen the vehicle or met with the
respondent’s agents and it is therefore a contract concluded under an organised distance
sales scheme.
[26]
The consequence of this is that the respondent was therefore obliged to comply with
Schedules 2 and 3 to the 2013 Regulations which require that the appellant is provided with
information about how to access the whole terms and conditions of the contract.  This would
have included ensuring that he was aware that he was liable to pay the whole contract price.
While it is not clear from the limited information available  that the respondent complied
with these requirements this does not form part of the appellant’s grounds of appeal.
[27]
On the assumption that the respondent did provide the appellant with the required
information and it was clear to the appellant that he was under an obligation to pay the

13

entire contract price the appellant was obliged to complete the purchase of the vehicle
subject to his 14 day cancellation rights in accordance with Regulations 29 to 34 of the
2013 Regulations.  The effect of Regulation 33(1)(a) is that in the event of cancellation, any
obligations incumbent upon the parties fell away.  In turn, the appellant was entitled to
insist upon a refund of the deposit as a payment received from the appellant pursuant to the
cancelled contract.
[28]
The 2013 Regulations applied to the party’s contract as a distance contract.  The
appellant is entitled to a refund of the deposit as he validly exercised his right to cancel,
which engaged his right to a refund under Regulation 33(1)(a).  He was not obliged to
provide any reason for his decision to cancel.  This being so, the sheriff’s second question
falls to be answered in the affirmative.  The sheriff deals with this issue at paragraphs 25 -27
of his appeal report and concedes that the Regulations do apply, particularly Regulation 34,
and had this been brought to his attention he would have allowed the matter to proceed to
proof and would not have dismissed the claim.  Accordingly the sheriff has fallen into error
which then had an impact on his further decisions in the case and the outcome for the
appellant.

Dismissal under rule 1.8(11)
[29]
In terms of this rule the sheriff may dismiss the appellant’s claim if it is obvious, it
had no real prospect of success.  That power must be read in line with simple procedure
being designed to provide a speedy, inexpensive and informal way to resolve disputes
(simple procedure rule 1.1(1)), that cases are to be resolved as quickly as possible and at the
least expense to the court (rule 1.2(1)) and the spirit of simple procedure which requires
candour from the parties and compliance with the orders of the sheriff regarding the

14

lodging of documents (Cabot Financial Ltd v Williams [2025] SAC (Civ) 38, at paras [26] - [28]).
Simple procedure is supposed to be simple and not difficult:  Cabot Financial UK Ltd v
Bell 2024 SC 91.
[30]
However, the power must also be read in line with the requirement for informality
being only as is appropriate, commensurate to the complexity of the issues (simple
procedure rule 1.2(2)) and the need to consider the threshold set by rule 1.8(11).  The sheriff
must only exercise the power where it is obvious there are no real prospects of success.
That term is not defined for the purposes of the simple procedure rules.  Some guidance
may be derived from the use of the same words in section 27B of the Court of Session
Act 1988 which was brought into force around the same time as the wording in rule 1.8(11).
