invited me to find that there was no such contract entered into and that the defender
acquired the vehicle from the pursuer by way of gift.
[33]
Mr Harrison also raised an esto point and suggested that if I determined the pursuer
had loaned money to the defender I could also conclude the loan was qualified by becoming
payable only upon the defender’s receipt of the expected inheritance referred to in evidence.
[34]
Mr McSherry objected to the esto position proposed by Mr Harrison, on the basis that
it was not raised in the written pleadings before the court and the pursuer had no notice of
such a position.  In this regard I accepted Mr Harrison’s submission that evidence on this
point was explored during the course of the proof without objection.
[35]
In the event I did not require to consider this point further given I do not accept upon
the evidence that a contract was entered into between the parties.
[36]
Finally, in his written submissions Mr McSherry invited me to make a finding in fact
that neither of the parties “are, or have ever been, qualified solicitors enrolled to practice

11
Scots law”.  Whilst I am sure this is indeed the case, neither party specifically confirmed this
in evidence and so I cannot properly make a finding in fact to that effect.
[37]
Mr McSherry also made much of this fact throughout his submissions but in my
view this has no material bearing on the question of whether or not a contract was entered
into between the parties.
[38]
In respect of the expenses of the action Mr McSherry and Mr Harrison were agreed
that expenses followed success.

Discussion
[39]
In addition to lodging written submissions parties’ agents also lodged lists of
authorities, and again I am obliged to them for their assistance in this regard.
[40]
The pursuer sets out to prove that in or around September 2022 the parties agreed
that the pursuer would purchase the vehicle, the defender would pay a sum equal to the
purchase price to the pursuer and that ownership of the vehicle would pass to the defender
upon payment of that sum in full.
[41]
Payment not having been made, the pursuer further avers the defender is in breach
of contract, albeit he does not seek compensation or payment of any further sums beyond
the purchase price of the vehicle.
[42]
The pursuer’s position in evidence was that the defender had represented to him that
she was the named beneficiary in the estate of a third party and that payment of the
purchase price of the car would be made upon receipt of this inheritance.  It is averred at
article three that the defender told the pursuer she was not a beneficiary in December 2023
and that, there being no basis to defer the date for making payment of the purchase price,
the sum due to the pursuer immediately became payable.

12
[43]
One difficulty for the pursuer is that he conceded in evidence that no discussion ever
took place between the parties as to what would happen if the defender did not receive the
inheritance upon which the purported contract is based.  It seems to me that if a contract
was entered into in the level of detail averred by the pursuer this would have been the
subject of discussion.
[44]
Another difficulty is that I found the pursuer’s evidence to be contradictory and
vague.  My impression of the pursuer’s evidence was that it was self-serving in the extreme,
particularly in circumstances where it was not supported by the terms of his own text
messages to the defender.
[45]
In all the circumstances I am not satisfied that a contract was entered into between
the parties and accordingly no sums are due by the defender to the pursuer.
[46]
I accept Mr McSherry’s submission that money lent is repayable on demand (The
Law of Contract in Scotland, McBryde, 3rd Ed Paragraph 24-21) but in this case no money
was “lent”.  Rather, a vehicle purchased by the pursuer was delivered by him to the
defender in circumstances where he was well aware she could not afford to purchase the
vehicle herself.
[47]
I do not accept the submission made on behalf of the pursuer that the text messages
sent by the defender to the pursuer amount to a recognition of an obligation to repay money
to the pursuer.  As I have indicated above, I have interpreted these messages as the
defender’s recognition that in all likelihood the pursuer would not have gifted her the
vehicle if he had appreciated their relationship would break down so soon afterwards.
[48]
I am satisfied that the purchase of the vehicle was a generous gesture on the part of
the pursuer in the context of a romantic relationship with the defender and that he presented
the vehicle to her as a gift.

13
[49]
In reaching this conclusion I fully appreciate that there is a strong presumption
against donation in Scots Law which “requires very strong and unimpeachable evidence to
overcome it”(Sharp v Paton (1883) 10R 1000 and Brownlee’s Exectrix v Brownlee 1908 SC 232).
[50]
However, I note that Brownlee concerned an entry in a formal account.  Clearly that is
not the position here.  The subject matter of the dispute between the parties is not a specific
sum of money paid by the pursuer to the defender but a tangible asset which was delivered
to her by him.
[51]
Mr Harrison relied upon a number of authorities which he suggested “taken
cumulatively” suggested an argument by analogy that the circumstances of this case
justified a presumption for donation.  He specifically indicated that these circumstances
were (i) a romantic relationship; (ii) a marked financial imbalance between the parties with
motivation to donate; (iii) a relatively modest sum involved and (iv) there being no
document of debt evidencing a loan.
[52]
I agree with Mr Harrison that the relationship between the parties is relevant.  Gloag
and Henderson The Law of Scotland (14th ed.)Vol 1 suggests that: “The presumption against
donation is less strong between husband and wife while relations are harmonious”.  Here,
the donation took place at a time when the parties were in a romantic relationship and there
was no suggestion it was not harmonious at the time the pursuer delivered the vehicle to the
defender.
[53]
Given the parties’ respective means were not detailed in the record I heard no
evidence in this regard and cannot be satisfied that there was a marked imbalance in the
parties’ relative means.  However, I am prepared to accept that the donation was “relatively
modest” as submitted by Mr Harrison, particularly given the pursuer’s evidence that he had

14
sold property in England and had a surplus of funds available to him at the time he
purchased the vehicle.
[54]
The vehicle was purchased by the pursuer and delivered to the defender in the
circumstances I have described.  As outlined in Gloag and Henderson The Law of Scotland
(above) paragraph 13.34: “All the circumstances surrounding the alleged donation will be
considered and clear proof is required.”
[55]
In this case I have carefully considered the circumstances in which the pursuer
acquired the vehicle and delivered it to the defender.  I have concluded that no discussion
took place during the parties’ relationship which had any bearing upon a liability on the
part of the defender to repay the pursuer the cost of the vehicle and I am satisfied that any
discussions on this point only took place after the relationship broke down.
[56]
I note a further passage in Gloag and Henderson (above) paragraph 13.35 which
states: “Proof of animus donandi is necessary but not sufficient to effect a valid donation.  In
addition, delivery or its equivalent is required to transfer ownership to the donee.”
[57]
Here, I am not only satisfied that the vehicle was delivered by the pursuer to the
defender, but also that the defender clearly became the owner and user of the vehicle
thereafter and was registered as the keeper of same.
[58]
The fact that delivery of the item was followed by the breakdown of the parties’
romantic relationship does not render the cost of the vehicle repayable, whether on demand
or upon the occurrence of a particular event.
[59]
Overall, my clear impression of the evidence is that the pursuer purchased the
vehicle and delivered it to the defender as a “grand gesture” during the parties’ relationship.
Obviously he did not anticipate that the relationship would break down after such a short
time, and perhaps understandably he now regrets having done so.

15

Decision
[60]
In light of the above I am satisfied that the pursuer purchased the vehicle and
delivered it to the defender as a gift in the context of a generous gesture made during the
course of a harmonious romantic relationship between the parties.
[61]
Accordingly, I will dismiss the pursuer’s crave.

Expenses
[62]
The position in respect of the expenses of the action was agreed as set out above and
I will find the pursuer liable to the defender in the expenses of the action.
